lesson.title: 20 Hz to 20 kHz: The Frequency Window of Human Hearing
lesson.summary: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, a frequency window that sets the target range for every piece of audio electronics built to reproduce sound for people.
lesson.body:
Frequency measures how many complete cycles of a periodic signal occur per second, in hertz. Sound is a mechanical pressure wave, but the ear converts it into an electrical nerve signal, and like any physical sensor, the ear only responds to a limited range of frequencies. For a typical young, healthy human, that range is commonly given as approximately 20 Hz at the low end to approximately 20,000 Hz, or 20 kHz, at the high end. Below about 20 Hz, vibrations may be felt as pressure or rumble rather than heard as a tone. Above about 20 kHz the sound is called ultrasound, and while some animals such as dogs and bats can perceive frequencies well beyond that upper limit, humans generally cannot.

It is useful to describe the hearing range not just in hertz but in octaves, since human pitch perception is closer to logarithmic than linear, meaning each doubling of frequency sounds like one equal step up in pitch. The number of octaves between 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz is found from log base 2 of the ratio of the two frequencies: log2(20,000 / 20) = log2(1,000) = 9.97, so human hearing spans just under 10 octaves. Compare that to a piano keyboard, which covers about 7 octaves, and you can see that human hearing extends noticeably beyond the range of a full piano.

The 20 Hz to 20 kHz figure is an idealized outer boundary, not a guarantee for every listener. High frequency sensitivity in particular tends to decline with age and with exposure to loud sound over time, so many adults cannot actually hear all the way up to 20 kHz even though the textbook range still cites it as the standard reference. This is why the human hearing range is treated as a design target for audio equipment, covered next, rather than a promise about what any one listener will perceive.
